The Mataram kingdom, also called Medang, was a Hindu-Buddhist kingdom in Central Java, later East Java, from the 8th to the early 11th century. It built both Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument in the world, and Prambanan, a great Hindu temple.

King Sanjaya founded it; his inscription of 732 marks its start. In the late 8th century the Buddhist Shailendra dynasty dominated the kingdom, while Hindu lords of Sanjaya's line held power too. Its wealth came from wet rice grown on the volcanic plains around Mount Merapi, and later from trade.

Its temples, all near modern Yogyakarta:

  • Borobudur, a stepped Buddhist monument of about 800, its galleries lined with carved panels telling the Buddha's lives.
  • Kalasan and Sewu, Buddhist temples of the same age.
  • Prambanan, about 850, a Hindu complex to Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, with the Ramayana carved around its walls.

The Javanese retelling of that epic, the Kakawin Ramayana, comes from the same era. The kingdom had links to Srivijaya on Sumatra and influence as far as Bali and southern Thailand.

Around 929 the court moved to East Java, perhaps after an eruption of Merapi or for trade. In 1016 its capital was destroyed in an attack by a vassal, Wurawari, possibly backed by Srivijaya. The king's son-in-law Airlangga rebuilt a kingdom in East Java. The Central Javanese temples were left to the jungle and the ash.
